title: Nursing Fundamentals
summary: An introduction to core nursing concepts: the nurse's role and ethics, vital signs, patient safety and hygiene, fluid balance, safe medicine administration and communication with SBAR. Educational only; clinical practice needs accredited training.
audience: Prospective nursing students, care assistants, community health workers and family carers

lessons.title: The nurse's role and professional ethics

body.p: Nurses care for people across their lives, in hospitals, clinics, homes, schools and communities. They assess patients, plan and give care, give medicines, educate patients and families, coordinate with other professionals and advocate for patients' needs. Nursing combines science, practical skill and compassion.

steps: Assess: collect information through history, observation and measurement.
Diagnose: identify the patient's health problems and needs.
Plan: set goals with the patient and choose interventions.
Evaluate: check whether goals were met and adjust the plan.

list: Respect dignity, privacy and cultural and religious beliefs.
Obtain informed consent before procedures.
Keep information confidential, sharing only with those involved in care.
Act in the patient's best interest and avoid harm.
Work within your scope of practice and follow your nursing council's code of conduct.

body.tip: This course introduces nursing concepts. Clinical practice requires accredited training, supervised placements and registration with your national nursing council.

body.p: Vital signs show how the body's essential systems are working. Trends over time matter more than single readings, and abnormal results must be reported according to local protocols, often using early-warning scores.

list: Temperature: about 36.1 to 37.2 °C (methods differ; fever is usually 38 °C or above).
Pulse: about 60 to 100 beats per minute. Counting 18 beats in 15 seconds gives 18 x 4 = 72 per minute; count a full minute if the rhythm is irregular.
Respiratory rate: about 12 to 20 breaths per minute, counted without the patient noticing.
Blood pressure: below about 120/80 mmHg is optimal; persistently 140/90 or above suggests hypertension. Mean arterial pressure for 120/80 is about (120 + 2 x 80) / 3 = 93.3 mmHg.
Oxygen saturation (SpO₂): usually 95 to 100% in healthy adults.

body.p: Children and older adults have different normal ranges; always use age-appropriate charts. Also observe skin colour, alertness, pain, urine output and how the patient looks and feels: "looks unwell" is important information.

body.tip: Never record a value you did not measure. If a reading seems wrong, recheck it with another device.

body.p: Patient safety means preventing avoidable harm during care. Common risks include infections, falls, pressure injuries, medication errors and misidentification.

list: Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact is the single most important infection-prevention action.
Confirm identity with at least two identifiers (name and date of birth or hospital number) before care or medicines.
Assess fall risk; keep beds low, call bells within reach and floors dry.
Prevent pressure injuries by changing position regularly (often every 2 to 4 hours for at-risk patients), keeping skin clean and dry and using pressure-relieving surfaces.
Use safe moving and handling techniques and equipment to protect patients and staff.

body.p: Help with washing, mouth care, eating and toileting while encouraging independence. Close curtains, explain what you are doing, and ask about pain regularly using a pain scale (for example 0 to 10). Good nutrition and hydration support healing.

body.tip: Report near-misses as well as incidents; they show where systems need fixing before someone is harmed.

body.p: The body needs a balance of fluid intake and output. Dehydration and fluid overload are both dangerous, especially for children, older people and patients with heart or kidney disease.

A fluid balance chart records all intake (oral drinks, tube feeds, intravenous fluids) and all output (urine, vomit, drains, diarrhoea). Example over 24 hours: intake 1200 mL oral + 800 mL IV + 400 mL tube feed = 2400 mL; output 1500 mL urine + 400 mL drain = 1900 mL. The balance is +500 mL (positive).

list: Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, dark and reduced urine, rapid pulse, low blood pressure, confusion.
Signs of overload: swelling, breathlessness, crackles in the lungs, rising weight.
Very low urine output should be reported promptly according to local guidelines.
Daily weights are a useful check of fluid status.

body.tip: Record fluids as they happen, not from memory at the end of a shift.

body.p: Giving medicines is a core nursing responsibility with real risk of harm. Nurses follow the "rights" of medication administration and local policies.

list: Right patient: check identity with two identifiers.
Right medicine: check the name against the prescription.
Right dose: check calculations; have high-risk calculations double-checked.
Right route: oral, IV, intramuscular and so on.
Right time and frequency.
Right documentation, immediately after giving.
Also: right reason, right to refuse, and checking allergies.

body.p: Before giving a medicine, know what it is for, its usual dose, common side effects and what to monitor. Question any prescription that seems wrong; never give a medicine you are unsure about.
Store medicines correctly: some need refrigeration, and controlled drugs need locked storage and two-person checks. Dispose of sharps immediately in a sharps container.

body.tip: Avoid interruptions during medicine rounds; distraction is a major cause of medication errors.

body.p: Clear communication saves lives. Many serious incidents involve information lost between staff, especially at shift changes and transfers.

list: Situation: what is happening now ("Mr Banda in bed 4 has a respiratory rate of 28").
Background: relevant history and treatment.
Assessment: what you think the problem is.
Recommendation: what you need ("Please review him within 20 minutes").
Write clearly, factually and promptly, with date, time and signature.
Record observations, care given, the patient's response and any changes.
Never alter records without following correction rules; electronic records log every change.
Use only approved abbreviations to avoid errors.

body.p: Talk with patients in plain language, check their understanding by asking them to explain back, and involve families where the patient agrees. Use trained interpreters where needed.

body.tip: If it was not documented, it was not done: legally and professionally, the record is the evidence of care.
